items.followUp: What is the difference between a bonding pair and a non-bonding pair of electrons?

rubric.why: Identifies that a lone pair belongs to one atom and is not shared.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the pair is not shared and remains on one atom.

rubric.why: Identifies that a bond pair is shared between atoms.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the pair is shared to form a covalent bond.

modelAnswer: A lone pair of electrons is not shared with another atom and remains on one atom.
A bond pair of electrons is shared between two atoms to form a covalent bond.

items.followUp: Explain how a double covalent bond is formed and give an example.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond involves sharing three pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award for specifying that three pairs of electrons are shared between the atoms.

rubric.why: Nitrogen molecule is a standard example of a triple covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award for identifying N₂ or an equivalent triple-bond example.

modelAnswer: A triple covalent bond is formed when two atoms share three pairs of electrons.
For example, two nitrogen atoms share three pairs of electrons to form N₂ (N≡N).

items.followUp: What is the difference between polar and non-polar covalent bonds in how electrons are shared?

rubric.why: Polar covalent bonds involve unequal sharing of electrons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the shared electrons are unequally distributed.

rubric.why: Non-polar covalent bonds involve equal sharing of electrons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the shared electrons are equally distributed.

modelAnswer: In a polar covalent bond, the shared electrons are unequally distributed between the bonded atoms.
In a non-polar covalent bond, the shared electrons are equally distributed between the bonded atoms.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of evaporation when the temperature of a liquid is increased?

rubric.why: The rate of evaporation increases as temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the effect of temperature on evaporation.
rubric.how: Award for saying that higher temperature increases the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: Higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy, allowing more to escape from the surface.
rubric.description: Explains the effect in terms of particles.
rubric.how: Award for linking increased kinetic energy with more molecules escaping into vapour.

modelAnswer: As the temperature of a liquid increases, its rate of evaporation increases.
The molecules gain kinetic energy, so more molecules can escape from the liquid's surface into the vapour.

items.followUp: How can the boiling point be used to distinguish a pure substance from a solution?

rubric.why: A pure liquid has a definite boiling point at a given pressure.
rubric.description: States the boiling behaviour of a pure liquid.
rubric.how: Award for identifying its fixed or definite boiling point.

rubric.why: A solution generally boils over a range of temperatures rather than at one fixed temperature.
rubric.description: States the boiling behaviour of a solution.
rubric.how: Award for stating that its boiling point is not fixed or that it boils over a range.

modelAnswer: A pure liquid has a fixed, definite boiling point at a given pressure.
A solution does not have a fixed boiling point and generally boils over a range of temperatures.

items.followUp: Define a strong electrolyte and give one example.

rubric.why: An electrolyte conducts electricity in molten or aqueous form because it has mobile ions.
rubric.how: Award for linking electrical conduction in solution or molten form to ions.
Award for naming any two suitable electrolytes.

modelAnswer: An electrolyte is a substance that conducts electricity in aqueous solution or in the molten state because it contains mobile ions.
Examples include sodium chloride (NaCl) and hydrochloric acid (HCl).

items.followUp: Write any two physical characteristics of non-metals.

rubric.why: Any one valid physical characteristic earns this mark.
rubric.description: Gives one physical characteristic of metals.
rubric.how: Award for naming any one: lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, or a good conductor of heat or electricity.

rubric.why: A second valid physical characteristic earns this mark.
rubric.description: Gives a second physical characteristic of metals.
rubric.how: Award for a different valid characteristic from the first.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally malleable (can be beaten into sheets).

items.followUp: Why are alkaline earth metals less reactive than alkali metals?

rubric.why: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell.
rubric.description: Compares the valence electrons of alkali metals.
rubric.how: Award for stating that an alkali metal has one valence electron.

rubric.why: Alkali metals lose one electron more readily than alkaline earth metals lose two.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that losing one electron is easier than losing two, or giving the lower ionization energy of alkali metals.

modelAnswer: Alkali metals have one electron in their outermost shell, whereas alkaline earth metals have two.
Alkali metals lose their single valence electron more readily; alkaline earth metals must lose two electrons, which requires more energy.
